C004.subject: rising economic inequality
C004.object: protest and voting among the poor in democratic rapidly developing economies when inequality is perceived as illegitimate due to corruption
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: rising economic inequality protest and voting among the poor in democratic rapidly developing economies when inequality is perceived as illegitimate due to corruption]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-national panel data on voter turnout and protest events in Brazil and India (e.g., from V-Dem or World Values Survey) merged with corruption perception indices (e.g., Transparency International) and Gini coefficients — This would allow direct testing of whether higher inequality combined with high corruption correlates with lower political participation among the poor, controlling for other factors.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or survey-based studies measuring perceived legitimacy of inequality and its effect on political efficacy and protest intention among low-income populations in rapidly developing democracies — Such micro-level evidence can isolate the causal mechanism of disillusionment and learned helplessness, testing whether perceived corruption-driven illegitimacy depresses participation.

[PATH:theoretical] Comparative case studies of social movements or electoral behavior in regions with high corruption and inequality (e.g., urban slums in Mumbai or favelas in Rio de Janeiro) that examine narratives of futility and disengagement — Qualitative insights can elaborate the hypothesized mechanism of learned helplessness and identify scope conditions not captured by quantitative data.

scope.domain: democratic contexts with high corruption (e.g., Brazil, India)

C005.subject: rising economic inequality
C005.object: protest and voting among the poor in democratic rapidly developing economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: rising economic inequality protest and voting among the poor in democratic rapidly developing economies]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey data on voter turnout and protest participation among low-income groups in Brazil and India (e.g., from the Brazilian Electoral Study, CSES, or the Indian National Election Study) combined with income inequality indices (Gini coefficients) over time — Directly tests whether rising inequality correlates with decreased voting and protest among the poor, controlling for other factors, in the specified contexts and time period.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of social movements and political engagement among the urban poor in São Paulo and Mumbai, focusing on periods of rapid economic growth and rising inequality post-1990s — Provides qualitative evidence on mechanisms (e.g., demobilization via clientelism, repression, or disillusionment) that quantitative data may miss, helping to confirm or refute the causal pathway.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical literature on political inequality and resource mobilization, e.g., works by Schlozman, Verba, and Brady on participatory inequality, or Piketty on capital and democracy — Frames the hypothesis within established theories of how economic resources affect political participation, offering testable predictions and identifying scope conditions for demobilization in rapidly developing democracies.

C006.subject: rising economic inequality
C006.object: state-sponsored civic organization membership among elites in authoritarian-leaning rapidly developing economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: rising economic inequality state-sponsored civic organization membership among elites in authoritarian-leaning rapidly developing economies]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey data on elite membership in state-sponsored organizations (e.g., Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, Indonesian Chamber of Commerce) linked to income and wealth inequality metrics (e.g., Gini coefficient) over 1990-2025. — Directly tests whether rising inequality correlates with increased elite participation in state-linked civic bodies, controlling for economic growth and political regime stability.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of elite behavior during inequality spikes in authoritarian-leaning economies (e.g., China post-2008, Indonesia post-1998 reformasi) using archival records, interviews, and organizational membership rosters. — Provides qualitative evidence of causal mechanisms (loyalty signaling, privilege preservation) and temporal dynamics, addressing the disputed mechanism of elite capture under redistribution threat.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal models of elite-state bargaining under inequality (e.g., Acemoglu-Robinson framework adapted for authoritarian civic organizations), tested with agent-based simulations calibrated to Chinese or Indonesian data. — Clarifies logical conditions under which inequality drives elite co-optation into state-sponsored groups, helping to resolve disputed causal direction and scope conditions.

scope.domain: authoritarian or hybrid regimes (e.g., China, Indonesia)

qualifier.mechanism: elite capture of civic space to signal loyalty and secure privileges under threat of redistribution

C007.subject: rising economic inequality
C007.object: turnout and membership in civic organizations in authoritarian-leaning rapidly developing economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: rising economic inequality turnout and membership in civic organizations in authoritarian-leaning rapidly developing economies]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative survey data from World Values Survey (WVS) and Asian Barometer Survey (2000-2020) on civic participation and inequality perception in China and Indonesia — These surveys provide individual-level data on membership in civic organizations and perceived economic inequality, enabling direct testing of the hypothesized relationship across time and within authoritarian contexts.

[PATH:empirical] Time-series analysis of Gini coefficients and registered civil society organization counts from China's Ministry of Civil Affairs and Indonesia's Ministry of Law and Human Rights (2000-2020) — Aggregate data on inequality (Gini) and official membership/registration figures for civic groups can reveal whether rising inequality correlates with increased organizational activity, controlling for state repression and economic growth.

[PATH:literature] Qualitative case studies of grassroots civic organizing in response to inequality in urban China and peri-urban Indonesia (e.g., labor NGOs, environmental groups) — In-depth studies can identify mechanisms (e.g., grievance, resource mobilization) linking inequality to civic engagement within authoritarian constraints, helping to interpret contradictory quantitative findings and refine the hypothesis.

scope.domain: authoritarian or hybrid regimes (e.g., China, Indonesia)
